fields.sample_size: case study of four Alabama Black Belt counties (Hale, Lowndes, Perry, Wilcox) using public-health and census data; no respondent sample
fields.effect_estimate: Argues from political philosophy that modern human rights include guaranteed access to sanitation; in Alabama's Black Belt (median incomes about $22,973-$34,679 vs state $46,472) public-health researchers found 65% (Hale) and 93% (Wilcox) of homes relying on unpermitted sewer systems, many discharging to the ground; nationally 470,000 households (about 1.2 million people) lack complete plumbing. Frames governmental neglect and weak regulation as failures to provide sanitation and guarantee public health. Doctrinal and descriptive; no effect estimates.
fields.study_design: doctrinal essay with a county-level descriptive case study (Alabama Black Belt)
fields.section: Full text: Introduction (human rights argument); Alabama Black Belt case study (income and sanitation table); Conclusions
fields.exact_location: Introduction (human rights argument); Alabama Black Belt case study (income and sanitation table); Conclusions

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a doctrinal essay on the human right to sanitation with an Alabama Black Belt county case study, read in full text 2026-10-04. Unpermitted sewage systems in 65-93% of surveyed homes in two counties are cited as evidence of governmental neglect. Descriptive, secondary data.
